title: Epidemiology and Evidence
tagline: Measuring disease, study designs, bias and confounding, trials, diagnostic tests and appraising evidence
summary: Good medicine rests on good evidence. This course covers how disease frequency and association are measured, observational study designs, bias, confounding and causal inference, the evaluation of diagnostic tests, randomised trials and the statistics clinicians need to read them, systematic reviews and meta-analysis, and how to appraise evidence, apply it to individual patients and use guidelines.
overview: Epidemiology studies how disease is distributed in populations and what determines it. Evidence-based medicine applies the same methods to clinical decisions: asking a precise question, finding the study design that can answer it, and reading the result without being misled. Clinicians meet both every day, in a trial result quoted in clinic, a screening invitation, or a new test advertised by its sensitivity. The difference between using evidence well and being misled by it is a set of skills that can be learned.

The course starts with measurement: prevalence, incidence, mortality and survival, standardisation, and the measures that compare groups. It then covers observational designs (cross-sectional, ecological, cohort and case-control studies), and the biases, confounding and causal reasoning that apply to all of them. Diagnostic testing is treated as applied Bayes' theorem: sensitivity, specificity, predictive values and likelihood ratios. The chapters on randomised trials and on statistics explain allocation, blinding, power, intention to treat, confidence intervals, p-values, the number needed to treat and hazard ratios. Systematic reviews and meta-analysis show how evidence is combined and graded, and the final chapter brings everything together in critical appraisal and the use of guidelines.

Every idea comes with a worked number: a person-time rate, a positive predictive value at two prevalences, a pooled risk ratio, an NNT for patients with different baseline risks. Each also comes with its typical failure: the ecological fallacy, Simpson's paradox, immortal time, regression to the mean, an odds ratio reported as a risk ratio, a funnel plot with missing studies. Interactive figures let you change prevalence, baseline risk and sample size and see how the answers change.
outcomes: Define and calculate prevalence, risk, incidence rate, mortality measures and standardised rates, and choose the right measure for a question.
Describe cross-sectional, ecological, cohort and case-control designs, calculate their measures of association, and explain when an odds ratio approximates a risk ratio.
Recognise selection bias, information bias and confounding, distinguish confounding from effect modification, and explain how design and analysis control them.
Apply Bradford Hill's viewpoints to judge whether an association is likely to be causal.
Calculate and interpret sensitivity, specificity, predictive values and likelihood ratios, and use Bayes' theorem to find post-test probabilities.
Explain randomisation, allocation concealment, blinding, sample size, non-inferiority and intention-to-treat analysis, and recognise their failures in published trials.
Interpret confidence intervals, p-values, absolute and relative risk reductions, numbers needed to treat and hazard ratios, and state what each does not mean.
Explain the methods of systematic reviews and meta-analysis, read a forest plot and funnel plot, and grade the certainty of evidence with GRADE.
Appraise a study for validity, results and applicability, individualise its results using a patient's baseline risk, and judge the trustworthiness of clinical guidelines.

history.title: Natural and political observations
history.detail: John Graunt analyses the London Bills of Mortality. He notes that more boys than girls are born, that many deaths occur in early childhood, and that London grows only through migration, founding the statistical study of populations.

history.title: Lind's scurvy experiment
history.detail: James Lind, a naval surgeon on HMS Salisbury, gives pairs of sailors with scurvy different remedies. The two given oranges and lemons recover quickly: an early controlled comparison of treatments, though not a randomised one.

history.title: The Broad Street pump
history.detail: John Snow maps cholera deaths around the Broad Street pump in Soho and compares cholera mortality in households supplied by two water companies, one drawing sewage-contaminated water from the Thames. William Farr's vital statistics at the General Register Office supply the denominators.

history.title: Yellow fever and the mosquito
history.detail: The US Army commission led by Walter Reed, with James Carroll, Aristides Agramonte and Jesse Lazear, tests Carlos Finlay's hypothesis in Cuba and shows that yellow fever is transmitted by the mosquito Aedes aegypti. Lazear dies of the disease during the work.

history.title: The streptomycin trial
history.detail: The Medical Research Council's trial of streptomycin for pulmonary tuberculosis, designed by Austin Bradford Hill, allocates patients by random numbers held centrally in sealed envelopes. It is widely regarded as the first properly randomised clinical trial.

history.title: Smoking and lung cancer
history.detail: Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill publish a case-control study linking smoking to lung cancer, and in 1951 begin the British Doctors Study, a cohort followed for fifty years. In 1965 Hill sets out his viewpoints for judging causation.

history.title: Effectiveness and Efficiency
history.detail: Archie Cochrane's book argues that health services should use treatments shown by randomised trials to work. In 1979 he criticises the profession for having no organised, regularly updated summary of all relevant randomised trials.

history.title: Evidence-based medicine
history.detail: The Evidence-Based Medicine Working Group, led from McMaster University by Gordon Guyatt, publishes its manifesto in JAMA, building on the clinical epidemiology of David Sackett and colleagues.

history.title: The Cochrane Collaboration
history.detail: Building on Iain Chalmers's systematic reviews of trials in pregnancy and childbirth, the Cochrane Collaboration is founded to prepare, maintain and disseminate systematic reviews of health care.

history.title: Trial registration
history.detail: The International Committee of Medical Journal Editors announces that its journals will publish trials only if they were registered before enrolment began, for trials starting recruitment from 1 July 2005, a major step against selective publication.

references.title: Gordis Epidemiology
references.authors: David D. Celentano and Moyses Szklo
references.note: Sixth edition. A clear introductory textbook covering measures of disease, study designs, bias, causation, screening and the evaluation of diagnostic tests, with many worked examples.

references.title: How to Read a Paper: The Basics of Evidence-Based Healthcare
references.note: Sixth edition. A short, practical guide to appraising trials, diagnostic studies, systematic reviews, guidelines and qualitative research.

references.title: Evidence-Based Medicine: How to Practice and Teach EBM
references.authors: Sharon E. Straus, Paul Glasziou, W. Scott Richardson and R. Brian Haynes
references.note: Fifth edition. The standard handbook of the five steps of evidence-based practice, with appraisal guides for therapy, diagnosis, prognosis and harm.

references.title: Users' Guides to the Medical Literature: A Manual for Evidence-Based Clinical Practice
references.authors: Gordon Guyatt, Drummond Rennie, Maureen O. Meade and Deborah J. Cook (eds)
references.note: Third edition. The JAMA Evidence guide to reading and applying the medical literature, including the GRADE approach.

references.title: Essential Medical Statistics
references.authors: Betty R. Kirkwood and Jonathan A. C. Sterne
references.note: Second edition. A thorough account of the statistics used in medical research, from confidence intervals to regression and survival analysis.

references.title: Modern Epidemiology
references.authors: Timothy L. Lash, Tyler J. VanderWeele, Sebastien Haneuse and Kenneth J. Rothman
references.note: Fourth edition. The advanced reference on epidemiological methods, including causal inference, bias analysis and study design.

references.title: Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions
references.authors: Julian P. T. Higgins, James Thomas, Jacqueline Chandler and others (eds)
references.note: Second edition (version 6), updated online. The reference for review methods, risk of bias (RoB 2), meta-analysis and GRADE.
